list.title: When Do Larger Batches Help Scale LLM Reinforcement Learning?
list.desc: Larger batches expose more parallelism by processing more sequences per update, but under a fixed sample budget, they also leave fewer opportunities to update the model. When does this trade-off reduce wall-clock time-to-target in reinforcement learning? For large language models, answering this question requires accounting for the online generation of training trajectories and the computational asymmetry between generation and training. We develop a framework that connects samples-to-target with end-to-end throughput: a larger batch accelerates training only when its throughput gain exceeds its samples-to-target penalty. This framework also suggests a simple practical strategy—first establish approximate batch-size invariance, then optimize throughput within that regime. Experiments with GRPO and PPO show that learning-rate retuning approximately preserves sample-indexed learning trajectories over a bounded batch range. On fixed hardware, larger batches improve generation throughput by up to 2.29x, and our best measured GRPO configuration reaches the same validation target in 29% less time without additional GPUs.
list.author: RL Team
list.content:
![Batch scaling overview#100%#auto#center](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/71e4f885/2026090811213134_d0d291b9138b4878d3c3ddb2d3c7e34d.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1788837694;2104197694&q-key-time=1788837694;2104197694&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=262651f0542e41c3dfd99a3063f076a01ea47f04)

*!12 Figure 1. Think of training as climbing toward the same capability target. The summit is the shared validation target, each route is a different batch size, and each marker is one optimizer update. After learning-rate retuning, B, 2B, and 4B make similar progress per response, while higher throughput lets the larger batches reach the summit sooner. At 16B, however, the additional sample cost outweighs the throughput gain, so the apparently larger step becomes a slower route. The legend reports normalized time-to-target.!*

# Introduction

Pretraining gives large language models a new capability baseline; reinforcement learning determines how far they can continue to advance by learning through exploration and feedback in new environments and tasks. DeepSeek-R1 helped demonstrate how large-scale RL can develop strong reasoning capabilities with little labeled data.[^r1] With Grok 4, xAI pushed the computational scale further: it reported using Colossus, its 200,000-GPU cluster, to run reinforcement learning at pretraining scale, with more than an order of magnitude more compute than in its previous RL work.[^grok] As RL becomes a larger part of model development, its **efficiency** has increasingly large consequences for training budgets.

Consider an illustrative budget: 10,000 GPUs running continuously for 30 days, at an assumed USD 3 per GPU-hour, would cost **USD 21.6 million**. Reaching the same model quality in 10% less time would save **720,000 GPU-hours, or USD 2.16 million** under those assumptions. For a team operating its own cluster, those GPU-hours become capacity for the next experiment.

Where should we look for that gain? One place is a parameter that every training recipe already has: **batch size**. In practice, batch size enters two recurring decisions:

- **Batch-size tuning: adapting the recipe.** A larger model or a different accelerator type can make the old batch size and learning rate unsuitable. A small batch may underutilize the hardware, while a mismatched learning rate may slow or destabilize learning. The goal is to find a batch size and matching hyperparameters that learn reliably while using the available hardware efficiently.
- **Batch-size scaling: turning parallelism into faster learning.** If the same model receives more GPUs, can the batch grow with them and reach the target sooner? Even without more GPUs, can a larger generation batch use otherwise idle capacity?

Both decisions lead to the same practical question: **how do we find the batch size that reaches the target performance in the shortest wall-clock time?**

A larger batch can be either an accelerator or a speed bump. In our experiments, a moderately larger batch with learning-rate retuning preserves learning efficiency while improving throughput. But once the batch becomes too large, the additional sample cost can outweigh the throughput gain. Figure 1 depicts this contrast as different routes to the same summit: a larger batch often helps, but it does not always get the model to the target sooner.

**What scientific principle governs this transition from acceleration to slowdown**, and **can it be turned into a measurable criterion for selecting the batch size that minimizes time-to-target**? To answer this question, we analyze batch scaling under the joint constraints of training dynamics and hardware execution, revisiting LLM RL scaling from first principles. This calls for the co-design of training algorithms and infrastructure. Our[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29296)develops the resulting framework.

# From Classical Batch Scaling to LLM Reinforcement Learning

> **How far can we usefully increase the batch?**

The modern large-batch story first became visible as an engineering breakthrough. In 2017, Goyal et al. trained ResNet-50 on ImageNet in one hour using 256 GPUs and a batch of 8,192, while preserving small-batch accuracy through linear learning-rate scaling and gradual warmup.[^goyal] The result showed that, with the right recipe, a larger batch could turn hardware parallelism into a dramatic reduction in wall-clock time. It also sharpened the next question: 

> **how far can this scaling remain effective?**

McCandlish et al. (2018) connected the point of diminishing returns to the gradient noise scale.[^mccandlish] Shallue et al. (2019) showed that useful data parallelism depends on the workload and that fair batch-size comparisons require hyperparameter tuning.[^shallue] The practical implication is simple: doubling the samples per update does not necessarily halve the updates needed to reach the same target.

A closely related question is whether changing the batch can preserve learning from a fixed number of samples. Hilton, Cobbe, and Schulman (2022) studied this as **batch-size invariance for policy optimization**: after adjusting the relevant hyperparameters, different batch sizes should produce similar learning behavior at equal sample counts.[^invariance] This is both a useful scaling intuition and a fair comparison principle: more samples should generally buy more capability, while the same cumulative sample budget should yield approximately the same capability across well-tuned batch sizes.

> **What changes in LLM RL?**

In supervised learning, examples already exist in a *fixed* dataset. Increasing the batch mainly changes gradient estimation, optimizer-update frequency, and training parallelism; the model does not have to produce its own training examples.

LLM RL adds an online loop. A Transformer agent first uses the current policy to sample responses or interact with an environment, producing trajectories and rewards. Those newly generated data are then consumed by forward passes, backward passes, and optimizer updates; the updated policy generates the next batch. **The model is therefore both the inference system that produces its training data and the learning system that consumes them.**

![LLM sampling and training share GPU computation#60%#auto#center](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/71e4f885/2026091516122958_72013eea4c7db8e6a838345f642a499e.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1789459950;2104819950&q-key-time=1789459950;2104819950&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=2fd9991431691c535c5753f36aaad19c90463bb0)

*!12 Figure 2. LLM reinforcement learning couples two GPU-intensive processes. Sampling uses autoregressive inference to produce responses and trajectories; training consumes those data to update the model. Batch size shapes both sides: generation batching determines how much inference work can run concurrently, while the training batch determines how much data each optimizer update consumes.!*

Both processes are GPU-intensive, but they exercise the hardware differently. Sampling generates one token at a time, repeatedly reads model weights, maintains KV caches, and schedules concurrent sequences. Training processes many token positions together but must store activations, compute gradients, and update optimizer states. As we show later, this computational asymmetry causes batch size to affect the two stages differently.

# Two Efficiencies, One Framework

Reaching the desired model quality sooner depends on two kinds of efficiency:

- **Sample efficiency** measures how much the model learns per training response. Batch size and its associated hyperparameters determine the progress obtained from a given sample budget.
- **System efficiency** measures how many training responses the full pipeline processes per second, accounting for generation, model updates, and waiting or synchronization.

Let $J$ denote validation performance, $N$ cumulative training responses, and $t$ elapsed time. Along a smooth approximation to a learning trajectory,

$$
\underbrace{\frac{dJ}{dt}}_{\text{Learning progress per second}}
=
\underbrace{\frac{dJ}{dN}}_{\text{Sample efficiency}}
\times
\underbrace{\frac{dN}{dt}}_{\text{System efficiency}}.
$$

If throughput doubles but learning progress per response halves, the two effects cancel. Batch size can change both factors, so we evaluate them jointly. This decomposition provides the conceptual starting point for our fixed-hardware analysis. Actual learning curves are noisy and evaluated at discrete checkpoints, so we use time-to-target for the empirical comparison.

Fix a validation target shared by all configurations. Let $N^\star$ be the number of training responses needed to reach it and $q$ the average end-to-end throughput over that interval. Then

$$
T=\frac{N^\star}{q}.
$$

Relative to a reference configuration, define the sample-cost ratio $r_N=N^\star/N_0^\star$ and throughput ratio $r_q=q/q_0$. Here, $r_N>1$ means the new configuration needs more responses to reach the target (i.e., a sample penalty), while $r_q>1$ means it processes more responses per second (i.e., a throughput gain).

### The criterion: throughput must outweigh sample cost

It is easy to see that a larger batch finishes sooner exactly when $r_q>r_N$.

::: success
Worked example
Suppose the reference configuration needs 100,000 responses at 1,000 responses per minute, so it reaches the target in 100 minutes. A larger batch needs 120,000 responses but processes 1,500 responses per minute. Then $r_N=1.2$, $r_q=1.5$, and

$$
\frac{T}{T_0}=\frac{r_N}{r_q} = \frac{1.2}{1.5}=0.8.
$$

The larger batch is 20% faster even though it is less sample-efficient, because the 50% throughput gain exceeds the 20% sample penalty. If throughput improved by only 10%, the ratio would instead be $1.2/1.1\approx1.09$, making the run about 9% slower.
:::

This relationship gives two complementary views:

- **In theory, compare throughput gain with sample penalty.** A larger batch reduces time-to-target only when $r_q>r_N$.
- **In practice, establish invariance before optimizing throughput.** Following the batch-size-invariance principle, retune batch-dependent hyperparameters and identify a range in which learning curves approximately align at equal cumulative response counts. Within that range, $r_N\approx1$, so higher end-to-end throughput translates more directly into shorter time-to-target. 

::: primary
Takeaway
Batch size affects both learning per response and end-to-end throughput. A larger batch reduces training time when its throughput gain outweighs any increase in the responses needed to reach the same quality. A simpler practical guideline is to first establish approximate batch-size invariance, then optimize throughput within that range.
:::

# Step 1: Preserve Learning per Sample

The first goal is to establish (approximate) batch-size invariance. Its implication is straightforward:
 doubling the batch should roughly halve the optimizer updates needed to reach the same model quality, leaving the total sample requirement approximately unchanged. 
 
 After separately retuning batch-dependent hyperparameters, a fair and intuitive scaling comparison should satisfy two expectations: 
- More samples should generally improve performance.
- At the same cumulative sample count, well-tuned runs with different batch sizes should achieve approximately the same performance.

Unfortunately, this does **not** happen automatically. A larger batch averages gradients over more responses, but it also gives the model fewer opportunities to update within a fixed sample budget. Preserving learning per response therefore requires retuning how far each update moves the policy.

**Retune the learning rate.** For Adam, we use the square-root rule as a starting point:

$$
\eta(B)=\eta_0\sqrt{\frac{B}{B_0}}.
$$

Here, $B_0$ and $\eta_0$ denote the reference batch size and learning rate. The rule is motivated by prior adaptive-optimizer scaling analysis.[^adam] We test it empirically while holding other optimizer hyperparameters fixed; jointly tuning more batch-dependent hyperparameters may further extend invariance.

To keep the comparison clean, we evaluate GRPO and PPO using our in-house training infrastructure. Both workloads use one global optimizer update per rollout batch, without minibatch subdivision or rollout reuse, avoiding additional tuning dimensions from minibatch size and optimization epochs.  Because training is stochastic and evaluation is noisy, we expect batch-size invariance to appear as approximate alignment, rather than exact overlap, between empirical learning curves.

### Finding I. Approximate invariance holds over a substantial, bounded range

**GRPO:** These experiments use Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 on a filtered subset of DAPO-MATH-17K, with $G=8$ responses per prompt. We evaluate mean@32 averaged over AIME 2024 and 2025. A training sample is a response retained after filtering and used in an optimizer update; each update contains $P$ retained prompt groups, giving $B_{\mathrm{train}}=PG$.

With learning-rate retuning, GRPO maintains approximately aligned sample-indexed learning curves across a 16-fold increase in prompt batch size. The left panel of Figure 3 shows this alignment from $P=64$ to $P=1024$ over the measured training window. At $P=2048$ and $P=4096$, the curves fall below this family at matched sample counts.

![figure2-batch-invariance.png](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/71e4f885/2026090823563361_f3819c4dc54707dc7200e0c9fbafecd3.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1788882995;2104242995&q-key-time=1788882995;2104242995&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=5cebf9aa20bc3b3a65c9c80916fe9b5ac4fcd6a8) 
*Figure 3. At fixed group size, retuned GRPO runs align over a bounded range of prompt batches. The largest batches depart from that family, and the decline in actor gradient norm flattens. The gray ±1-percentage-point band is a visual reference, not a confidence interval.*

The right panel of Figure 3 provides a complementary view of this departure. Across the approximately invariant range, actor gradient norms decrease roughly as $P^{-1/2}$. At $P=2048$ and $P=4096$, this decline becomes shallower, coinciding with the loss of learning-curve alignment in the left panel. This pattern is consistent with diminishing benefits from gradient averaging: beyond this range, adding more responses to each update no longer compensates as effectively for taking fewer updates. 

**PPO:** We use an internal Hunyuan policy model and value model, each with 3B active parameters, trained on an internal dataset mixing math, science, and logic tasks. Evaluation performance is averaged across the corresponding benchmarks. Here, each prompt retains one response, so $G=1$ and $B_{\mathrm{train}}=P$.

![figure5-ppo-invariance.png](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/71e4f885/2026090823570254_72679251353a7e9d1653749f891d862b.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1788883024;2104243024&q-key-time=1788883024;2104243024&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=80aea6fb3bf747c81413c0c89adc588c455d5070) 
*Figure 4. Batch scaling in PPO. Left: validation performance versus cumulative training responses. Right: actor and critic gradient norms across batch sizes.*

The left panel of Figure 4 shows approximately aligned sample-indexed learning curves for batches from 256 through 2048, while batch 4096 falls below this family. This provides complementary evidence that learning-rate retuning can approximately preserve learning per response over a bounded batch range in PPO.

The right panel reveals a difference between the actor and critic. Actor gradient norms decrease as the batch grows, with the decline becoming shallower at the largest batch. Critic gradient norms, by contrast, remain comparatively flat and noisy. These observations suggest that the actor and critic may have different useful batch scales. Given their distinct training objectives, understanding this difference and whether separate tuning can improve efficiency is an interesting direction for future work.

### Finding II. Total response count as the batch-size unit

In GRPO, we can enlarge the batch along two axes: sampling more prompts or more responses per prompt. Because responses within a group share the same prompt and contribute to group-relative advantages, these two choices need not reduce variance in the same way. Do they nevertheless produce similar learning behavior when the total response batch is held fixed?

We compare two pairs of configurations: $(P,G)=(128,8)$ versus $(64,16)$, both with 1,024 responses per update, and $(P,G)=(256,8)$ versus $(128,16)$, both with 2,048 responses per update. The figure denotes group size by $n$, corresponding to $G$ in our notation.

The left panel shows broadly similar learning trajectories, although the curves do not overlap at every checkpoint. The right panel shows a clearer pairing: configurations with the same total response batch have similar actor gradient norms, while the larger total batch produces consistently smaller norms. Together, these results support using total retained responses, $PG$, as the batch unit for the configurations tested.

![Clipboard_Screenshot_1789012202.png](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/71e4f885/2026091011534977_8e66a4bd347c404da4e3f880491d113b.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1789012429;2104372429&q-key-time=1789012429;2104372429&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=609efae6058ac830cff64182399ad38c63dba9ec)
*Figure 5. Group-size comparison in GRPO. Left: validation performance versus cumulative training responses. Right: actor gradient norms over the same training window. Solid lines correspond to 1,024 responses per update; dashed lines correspond to 2,048. Blue and orange distinguish group sizes of 8 and 16.*

### Finding III. Keeping the learning rate fixed breaks approximate batch-size invariance

In practice, adding GPUs often increases both data parallelism and the global batch. If the learning rate and other hyperparameters remain tuned for the smaller batch, training may still look stable—and may even look smoother because gradient noise is lower. But at the same cumulative response count, the larger batch has taken fewer optimizer steps and may not reach the same quality. Stable training therefore does **not** imply batch-size invariance; the larger batch may need substantially more responses to catch up.

We compare a reference configuration with $P=128$ and $\eta=10^{-6}$ against two configurations with $P=256$: one keeps the learning rate fixed, while the other increases it to $\sqrt{2}\times10^{-6}$ following the square-root rule. Group size is held fixed.

![Clipboard_Screenshot_1789012475.png](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/71e4f885/2026091011543675_19e6072bf0695bf76cb71eed4cd8bcc4.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1789012479;2104372479&q-key-time=1789012479;2104372479&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=cdec201de2913526930a518ceae39f1c44d7306d)
*Figure 6. Learning-rate control in GRPO. Left: validation performance versus cumulative training responses for the reference batch, a doubled batch with square-root learning-rate scaling, and a doubled batch with the learning rate fixed. Right: optimizer-update counts normalized to the reference first-hit count, illustrating how retuning brings the doubled batch closer to the ideal halving of updates.*

The left panel shows why retuning matters. With the scaled learning rate, the larger-batch run broadly follows the reference learning curve at matched sample counts. Keeping the learning rate fixed instead produces a substantial lag through much of training. Around 120K responses, for example, the fixed-learning-rate run scores approximately 74%, compared with roughly 77% for the reference and retuned runs.

The right panel quantifies the difference in optimizer updates. Exact batch-size invariance predicts that doubling the batch should halve the updates needed to reach the same target. The scaled-learning-rate run has a target-crossing interval of **0.50–0.67×** the reference first-hit count, consistent with the ideal **0.50×** at the available checkpoint resolution. The fixed-learning-rate run instead requires **0.75–0.83×**, substantially above that ideal.

::: primary
Takeaway
Learning-rate retuning approximately preserves learning per response over a bounded batch range in our GRPO and PPO experiments. In the GRPO group-size comparison, configurations with the same total response batch also show broadly similar learning trajectories and closely matched gradient norms. PPO likewise shows approximate invariance over a bounded range, but the actor and critic exhibit markedly different gradient-norm scaling as the batch grows.
:::

# Step 2: Improve Throughput Even on Fixed Hardware

Once learning per sample is approximately preserved, the next question is how to process those samples faster. A familiar approach is to add GPUs and increase data parallelism. But can a larger batch accelerate training without adding hardware? On the same devices, processing more responses per update might seem to simply take proportionally longer. In LLM RL, an opportunity comes from **generation–training computational asymmetry**.

- During autoregressive decoding, each sequence produces one new token at a time. At low concurrency, the GPU repeatedly reads model weights to process relatively few token vectors. More active sequences allow more tokens to share those weight transfers, so the number of responses can grow faster than the time needed to generate them.

- Training has a different execution pattern. Once responses are available, forward and backward passes process many token positions together, already exposing substantial parallelism. In this regime, increasing the batch mainly adds work. 

A simple local model summarizes this contrast:

$$
t_{\mathrm{gen}}(B_{\mathrm{gen}})\approx d_0+d_1B_{\mathrm{gen}},
\qquad
t_{\mathrm{train}}(B_{\mathrm{train}})\approx\gamma B_{\mathrm{train}}.
$$

Here, $B_{\mathrm{gen}}$ counts responses in the logical rollout batch, while $B_{\mathrm{train}}$ counts retained responses consumed by one optimizer update. Our experiments use asynchronous partial rollouts with $B_{\mathrm{gen}}=2B_{\mathrm{train}}$, so increasing the training batch also increases the generation batch. The intercept $d_0$ captures generation cost that can be amortized across responses: increasing the batch reduces this cost per response, whereas training time grows approximately in proportion to its batch size. Our[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29296)develops this intuition through a roofline view, explaining how batching changes arithmetic intensity and when execution is limited by memory bandwidth or compute. The simplified model above captures the resulting difference between generation and training costs.

The throughput gain depends on how the execution system translates a larger generation batch into active decoding concurrency, subject to scheduling and memory constraints. We therefore measure end-to-end throughput using retained training responses per second, including time spent on discarded responses, model updates, and pipeline overhead.

### Finding IV. Response-collection time grows sublinearly over the measured range

Figure 7 compares the increase in retained training responses with the increase in collection time, both normalized to the smallest batch. In both workloads, the blue response-count bars grow faster than the orange time bars. Their ratio gives the generation-stage throughput gain.

![figure6-generation-throughput.png](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/71e4f885/2026090823591270_60acf35352b316010a5c1b457540fc93.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1788883154;2104243154&q-key-time=1788883154;2104243154&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=c4af122b30ea8a98a786517038ef727d7b8ccdc2) 
*Figure 7. More responses need not take proportionally more collection time. On fixed hardware, a 4× batch increase raises generation-stage throughput by 2.29× in PPO and 1.36× in GRPO.*

In PPO, increasing the training batch from 256 to 1024 collects four times as many responses per optimizer update, while collection time increases from 39 to 68 seconds. Response-collection throughput therefore improves by $4/(68/39)=2.29\times$.

In GRPO, increasing $P$ from 128 to 256 improves generation-stage throughput by 1.31×; increasing it to 512 yields 1.36×. The small additional gain suggests that the available benefit is already flattening over this range.

::: primary
Takeaway
Generation and training scale differently with batch size: generation can amortize model-weight reads across more concurrent sequences, whereas training time grows approximately in proportion to the batch. When decoding has not yet saturated the hardware, doubling the generation batch generally increases collection time by less than 2×, improving generation throughput even without additional GPUs.
:::

# Step 3: Combine Two Critical Batches to Minimize Time-to-Target

The preceding results reveal two distinct limits to batch scaling in LLM reinforcement learning:
- **The critical generation batch** concerns system efficiency. It marks where generation throughput approaches its plateau for a fixed model, decoding engine, response-length distribution, and hardware allocation. Below this scale, increasing the batch can improve hardware utilization; beyond it, further batching yields little additional generation throughput.
- **The critical training batch** concerns sample efficiency. It marks the upper end of approximate batch-size invariance under learning-rate retuning. Within this range, larger batches need roughly the same number of responses to reach a given target. Beyond it, the benefit of averaging over more responses no longer fully compensates for taking fewer updates, increasing the sample requirement.

These two limits need not coincide. Figure 8 illustrates their distinct roles, with memory capacity imposing a separate constraint on feasible generation batches. Their interaction determines how far increasing the batch can reduce training time.

![Clipboard_Screenshot_1789019582.png](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/71e4f885/2026091013530224_dda9df2d9372a59a936f2bf8f8536add.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1789019585;2104379585&q-key-time=1789019585;2104379585&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=1d29eeb9d67a3f026e6a5d7bf7a928d94625162f)
*Figure 8. Two critical batch sizes. Left: generation throughput approaches a plateau. Right: learning per response remains approximately preserved under learning-rate retuning before declining at larger batches. Both curves are schematic.*

### From critical batches to training time

How do these limits combine to determine training time? Consider a coupled configuration in which generation and training batches increase together. Figure 9 illustrates the case where generation throughput plateaus before learning efficiency deteriorates. In this schematic, the generation plateau also limits further gains in end-to-end throughput, producing a near-optimal range of training batch sizes.

![Coupled batch scaling#600px#center](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/71e4f885/2026091013191098_eee2e3aee8f67952d5a27f93a44c88b1.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1789017553;2104377553&q-key-time=1789017553;2104377553&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=678a100caf9733bf8fab5ebbadc0e33ec2d37a27)
<div style="width: 600px; transform: translateX(-50%); margin-left: 50%; display: block;">
*!12 Figure 9. Schematic time-to-target when generation throughput saturates before sample efficiency deteriorates. The star marks the smallest batch on the near-optimal plateau.!*
</div>

This ordering produces three regimes:

- **Learning is preserved and throughput improves.** Increasing the batch reduces training time because the model needs approximately the same number of responses, while the system processes them faster.
- **Learning is preserved but throughput plateaus.** Further batching offers little additional speed. A range of batch sizes can therefore achieve similar training times.
- **The sample penalty dominates.** Once larger batches require more responses to reach the target, limited throughput gains can no longer compensate, and training time increases.

The ordering can also be reversed. If learning efficiency deteriorates before generation throughput plateaus, a larger batch can still finish sooner when its throughput gain outweighs the additional sample cost. 

### Empirical Observations

Figure 10 connects this reasoning to our GRPO experiments on fixed hardware, with $G=8$ and $P=128$ as the reference configuration.

![Clipboard_Screenshot_1789017161.png](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/71e4f885/2026091013124253_737a0bd9bd493c769cf101400160fbe6.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1789017165;2104377165&q-key-time=1789017165;2104377165&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=81e009c3fbd643046d3603bd4482937431c679b2)
*Figure 10. Normalized GRPO training time across prompt batch sizes. Blue points use square-root learning-rate scaling; the orange control keeps the learning rate fixed. All times are normalized to the $P=128$ reference. The star marks the best measured configuration.*

With learning-rate retuning, increasing $P$ from 128 to 512 and 1024 reduces normalized time-to-target to **0.74× and 0.71×**. At $P=1024$, the sample requirement remains unchanged while throughput improves by 41%, cutting training time from 11.90 to 8.42 hours—**29% less time without adding GPUs**.

Larger batches do not always help. At $P=2048$ and $P=4096$, a **60% increase in required responses** outweighs throughput gains of 30% and 36%, raising training time to **1.23× and 1.18×**.  The deciding factor is whether throughput gains compensate for additional sample cost.

# Conclusion

The criterion translates into two practical stages:

1. **Align learning per response.** For each candidate training batch, retune the learning rate (and other hyper-parameters), compare learning curves at equal cumulative response counts, and estimate the sample-cost ratio $r_N$ at a shared validation target.
2. **Measure the systems gain.** Within memory limits, tune generation batching or decoding concurrency, measure end-to-end throughput $q$, and select the feasible configuration that maximizes $q/r_N$. Recheck $r_N$ whenever systems changes alter learning behavior.

![algorithm-two-stage-v2.png](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/71e4f885/2026090823593928_f70506f147502883189db553d2849585.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1788883181;2104243181&q-key-time=1788883181;2104243181&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=b4da7c3dcd246703772f094a810d27305bf791bc) 

# Future Work

An interesting question is whether the useful batch range can be predicted, rather than rediscovered through expensive sweeps for every new setting. This requires a mechanistic understanding of why approximate batch-size invariance emerges, what determines its boundary, and why it eventually breaks. Learning-rate retuning is only a first step. A more complete scaling theory should explain how the relevant batch-dependent hyperparameters transfer across models, objectives, task distributions, and training stages.

The PPO results further suggest that batch size may not have a single universal meaning even within one training algorithm. The actor and critic optimize different objectives and exhibit different gradient-norm scaling behavior; they may therefore have different critical training batches. Understanding these distinct dynamics could motivate separate batch sizes, update schedules, or tuning rules for the two components.

At the systems level, our observations are specific to autoregressive Transformers, where token-by-token generation and parallel training place different demands on the hardware. Other architectures—including state-space, recurrent, or hybrid models—may shift this generation–training asymmetry and therefore have different critical batch scales. A model- and system-aware RL stack should account for these differences while decoupling generation concurrency from the optimizer batch, without overlooking the resulting trade-offs in queueing, policy staleness, and data freshness.

The broader goal is therefore not merely to tune batch size, but to develop a predictive, architecture-aware understanding of RL scaling—one that jointly explains training dynamics, hardware execution, and their interaction in determining time-to-target.

Today we're releasing Hy4 preview, our most capable model to date. It's a 770B-parameter model with 49B active parameters and a 1M-token context window, and it makes the biggest gains where the work is hardest: long-horizon software engineering, document-heavy office work, and scientific research.

# A new flagship generation
We scaled Hy4 preview on three fronts: model size, context length, and training data.  Stronger pre-training and a substantially larger post-training run compound into another step change in capability — the largest generation-over-generation gain we've measured, and enough to put Hy4 preview at the open-source frontier.

@@@space
height = 16
@@@

![Hy4 preview-bench.png](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/9a5ea02f/2026082721321326_51078c894df8469245775f1cab28d1af.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1787837538;2103197538&q-key-time=1787837538;2103197538&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=6835cdda2834895db514e16c6995bba3ee1f64f7)

# Built for productivity
We partnered with top experts inside Tencent — such as software engineers, game developers, finance analysts, and security experts — and built training data around the work they ship. The result is a model that gets meaningfully further on the tasks these teams run every day:
## Software engineering
Better at understanding, planning, debugging, and verifying long-horizon development tasks, with further gains in the visual taste and interaction quality of front-end work.

list.title: From LR to ELR: A Better Heuristic for Pretraining Dynamics
list.desc: Understanding pretraining dynamics is crucial for designing effective training hyperparameters for large language models (LLMs), particularly the learning rate (LR). However, LR does not always reflect how much the function represented by the model actually changes, and the optimal LR often shifts with model and data scale. In this post, we identify that the effective learning rate (ELR), which controls the directional changes of model weights, is a more intrinsic heuristic than LR as a tunable hyperparameter. Specifically, ELR delivers more accurate loss prediction under the multi-power law (MPL) model and transfers more reliably across model scales. More broadly, the ELR perspective guides the design of better schedules, which outperform conventional LR-schedule baselines.
list.author: Pretrain Team
list.content:
![Clipboard_Screenshot_1785920196.png](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/b729e183/2026080516563630_28c59be2fc21524ca77ae6700c813cc6.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1785920200;2101280200&q-key-time=1785920200;2101280200&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=b50863f4b82fb3771891afadc797f6f9cbb216c7) *!12 Figure 1. Modded-nanoGPT Track 3 optimization benchmark results.!* **!12 Our MuonH + minus-square-root schedule!** *!12 reaches the 3.28 validation loss target at step 3175, setting a new SOTA for MuonH.!* # Introduction When training Large Language Models (LLMs), the learning rate (LR) is often treated as the main knob controlling optimization speed. For a standard update on weight $\mathbf{w}_{t}$ at iteration $t$, $$ \begin{equation} \mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \underbrace{(1 - \eta_t \lambda)}_{\text{weight decay}} \mathbf{w}_{t} - \eta_t\; \texttt{Opt} (\underbrace{\nabla f(\textbf{w}_t)}_{\text{gradient}}),\tag{1} \end{equation} $$ the learning rate $\eta_t$ scales the optimizer's update $\texttt{Opt} (\nabla f(\textbf{w}_t))$, which often changes both the parameter's magnitude and direction [^ref1]. However, the widespread use of normalization layers introduces the scale-invariance[^ref_scale_invariance][^ref_scale_invariance_2] to many weights in LLMs: $$ \mathbf{w} \text{ is scale-invariant if }\quad f(c\,\mathbf{w}) = f(\mathbf{w}) \quad \forall c>0. $$ In scale-invariant weights, the direction of the weights matters more than their magnitude, yet the normal LR does not directly control these directional dynamics. Indeed, LR tuning is often challenging in LLM pretraining: the optimal LR can vary with architecture, model size, and data scale, often demanding practitioners to fit hyperparameter scaling laws for every new configuration. This motivates the notion of *angular update size (AUS)* [^ref6], which measures the directional change as the distance between unit-normalized weight matrices at consecutive steps: $$ \text{AUS} := \left\Vert \frac{\mathbf{w}_{t+1}}{\Vert\mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert} - \frac{\mathbf{w}_t}{\Vert\mathbf{w}_t\Vert} \right\Vert . $$ Prior studies [^ref1] [^ref2] [^ref_spherical] [^ref_intrinsic_lr] on AUS originate from analyses of weight decay, which shrinks the weight norm and thereby promotes directional changes. In this post, we focus on directly controlling the AUS during LLM training. Specifically, we rewrite the update rule in Eq. (1) as follows and explicitly control the AUS via the *effective learning rate (ELR)* $\eta_t^\star$ below: $$ \mathbf{w}_{t+1} = (1-\eta \lambda )\mathbf{w}_{t} - \eta^\star_t\frac{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t} \Vert\texttt{Opt}_t}{\Vert \texttt{Opt}_t \Vert}, \text{ where } \eta^\star_t := \frac{\eta\Vert \texttt{Opt}_t \Vert}{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t} \Vert} $$ Compared to LR, we show that ELR is a better heuristic as a tunable hyperparameter. We summarize our findings as follows: - Direct control of AUS naturally **leads to the recent Hyperball optimization** method [^ref_hyperball], in which LR implicitly serves as ELR. Matching the AUS trajectories of standard optimizers and their Hyperball variants produces nearly identical loss curves. - **ELR enables more accurate loss prediction** under the multi-power law (MPL) model [^ref_multi], and **optimal ELR transfers more reliably** across model widths and depths. - Inspired by the intrinsic patterns of AUS, we propose the minus-square-root schedule, which **improves the previous Track3-MuonH SOTA by 75 steps**, reaching the target loss of 3.28 in 3,175 steps. It also outperforms linear and WSD baselines in 6B-MoE training and across a scaling ladder. # AUS, ELR, and Hyperball Optimization **Defining AUS.** Let $\mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t} := \frac{\mathbf{w}_t}{\Vert\mathbf{w}_t\Vert}$, we define AUS through the directional update: $$ \mathrm{AUS} := \Vert \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t+1} - \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t} \Vert \approx \frac{\eta_t\Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^{\perp} \Vert }{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1} \Vert}, \text{ with } \texttt{Opt}_t^{\perp} = (I - \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_t\mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t}^\top) \texttt{Opt}_t. $$ +++ **Proof Sketch** Consider the update rule, we have: $$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{w}_{t+1} &= (1-\eta_t \lambda )\mathbf{w}_{t} - \eta_t \texttt{Opt}_t \\ &= \left((1-\eta_t\lambda) \Vert\mathbf{w}_{t} \Vert - \eta_t \langle \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_t, \texttt{Opt}_t\rangle\right) \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t} - \eta_t \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp \end{aligned}$$ Define $C = (1-\eta_t\lambda) \Vert\mathbf{w}_{t} \Vert - \eta_t \langle \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_t, \texttt{Opt}_t\rangle$, we have: $$\begin{aligned} \Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert= \Vert C \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t} - \eta_t \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp \Vert = \sqrt{C^2 + \eta_t^2 \Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp \Vert^2 } \end{aligned}$$ Thus, $$\begin{aligned}\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert^2 - C^2 &= \eta_t^2 \Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp \Vert^2 \\ (\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert - C) (\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert + C) &=\eta_t^2 \Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp \Vert^2 \\ \Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert - C&= \frac{\eta_t^2 \Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp \Vert^2 }{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert + C} \end{aligned}$$ Taking this back to the update rule, by normalizing the weights, we have: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t+1} &= \frac{C}{\Vert \mathbf{{w}}_{t+1}\Vert} \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t} - \frac{\eta_t}{\Vert \mathbf{{w}}_{t+1}\Vert} \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp\\\mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t+1} - \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t} &= \frac{C - \Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert}{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert} \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t} - \frac{\eta_t}{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert} \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp \\ \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t+1} - \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t} &= -\frac{\eta_t^2\Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp \Vert^2 }{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert (\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert + C)} \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t} - \frac{\eta_t}{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert} \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp\end{aligned}$$ For sufficiently small $\eta_t$, $$\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert + C \geq 2C \geq \Vert \mathbf{w}_t\Vert.$$ Hence, $$\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1} \Vert(\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert + C) \geq \frac{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t}\Vert}{2} \Vert \mathbf{w}_t \Vert = \frac{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t}\Vert^2}{2}.$$ Thus, $$\left\Vert \frac{\eta_t^2\Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp \Vert^2 }{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert (\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert + C)} \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t} \right\Vert \leq \frac{2\eta_t^2\Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp \Vert^2}{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t}\Vert^2}$$ Finally, $$\mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t+1} - \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t} = - \frac{\eta_t}{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert} \texttt{Opt}_t^\perp + \mathcal{O}(\eta_t^2).$$ +++ ![Clipboard_Screenshot_1785398566.png#320px #146px #float-right](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/b729e183/2026073016030443_0a853c68dc97c175ab80e690c1baef6a.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1785398587;2100758587&q-key-time=1785398587;2100758587&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=f21054b4649aeb79bebe49655f492a85fa939017) Let $\theta$ denote the angle between $\mathbf{w}_{t+1}$ and $\mathbf{w}_t$, the AUS is approximately $\sin \theta$: $$ \sin \theta = \frac{\Vert (I - \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t}\mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t}^\top)(\mathbf{w}_{t+1} - \mathbf{w}_t)\Vert}{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert} = \frac{\eta_t\Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^{\perp} \Vert }{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1} \Vert}. $$ That said, AUS captures the angular change in model weights, providing a faithful proxy for step size in scale-invariant models. Then, what happens if we control AUS directly? **Tuning ELR.** We decompose $\eta'_t := \frac{\eta_t\Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^{\perp} \Vert }{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1} \Vert}$ from a standard update: $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{w}_{t+1} &= (1-\eta \lambda )\mathbf{w}_{t} - \eta'_t \frac{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1} \Vert\texttt{Opt}_t}{\Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^{\perp}\Vert} \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \Vert \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t+1} - \mathbf{\widehat{w}}_{t} \Vert\approx\eta_t' \\ \end{aligned} $$ Under this rule, we tune $\eta_t'$ directly to control AUS. However, $\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1} \Vert$ is unavailable, and explicitly obtaining the orthogonal component $\texttt{Opt}_t^{\perp}$ introduces additional computational cost. To address these, we approximate the $\eta'_t$ with the notion of ELR, $\eta^\star_t := \frac{\eta_t\Vert \texttt{Opt}_t \Vert }{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t} \Vert}$, and the corresponding update rule changes to: $$ \begin{equation} \mathbf{w}_{t+1} = (1-\eta \lambda )\mathbf{w}_{t} - \eta^\star_t\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t}\Vert \texttt{N}(\texttt{Opt}_t), \text{ where } \texttt{N}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\mathbf{x}}{\Vert \mathbf{x} \Vert}. \tag{2} \end{equation} $$ This approximation relies on two assumptions: 1. $\Vert\mathbf{w}_{t+1} \Vert \approx \Vert\mathbf{w}_{t}\Vert$. Weight decay reduces the weight norm, while the optimizer update often expands it. As training progresses, these two effects gradually balance, and the weight norm becomes stationary. 2. $\langle \texttt{Opt}_t, \mathbf{w}_t\rangle \approx 0$. For a scale-invariant objective, the gradient is exactly orthogonal to the weights, i.e., $\langle \nabla f(\mathbf{w}_t), \mathbf{w}_t\rangle = 0$. Therefore, the gradient-based update is approximately orthogonal to the parameters, particularly in high-dimensional spaces. > Recently, manifold optimization has attracted growing interest in optimizer design [^ref_modular] [^ref_jianlin] [^ref_sso] [^ref_mano] , where each update is projected onto the tangent space of the target manifold. For example, consider a hypersphere embedded in Euclidean space; the tangent space at the current iterate consists of all vectors orthogonal to the current weight vector. Hence, our second assumption naturally holds. **Connecting Hyperball optimization.** Let us revisit our first assumption. The relation $\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1}\Vert \approx \Vert \mathbf{w}_t \Vert$ does not hold universally, especially at the beginning of the training. A direct fix is to enforce a fixed weight norm by design, i.e., $\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t}\Vert = \Vert \mathbf{w}_0 \Vert$. Consequently, weight decay becomes redundant: $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \Vert \mathbf{w}_{0} \Vert \cdot \texttt{N}\left(\mathbf{w}_{t} - \eta^\star_t\Vert \mathbf{w}_{0}\Vert \texttt{N}(\texttt{Opt}_t)\right). \end{aligned} $$ Notably, replacing $\Vert\mathbf{w}_0\Vert$ with a configurable hyperparameter $R$ leads to the recently proposed *Hyperball optimizers* [^ref_hyperball] $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{w}_{t+1} = R \cdot \texttt{N}\left(\mathbf{w}_t - \eta_t^\star R \cdot \texttt{N}(\texttt{Opt}_t) \right), \end{aligned} $$ which leads to 20-30% speedup over standard optimizers with weight decay as in Eq. (1). A similar idea dates back to *Van Laarhoven (2017)* [^ref2], who proposed fixing the weight norm to remove weight decay. Our derivation aligns with the motivation of Hyperball optimizers: its LR implicitly serves as the ELR, enabling direct control of AUS. To further validate its AUS control ability, we design a special experiment: - **Baseline.** We train a scale-invariant GPT-2 model (124M) with Adam/Muon and record the AUS at every update step. - **AUS as LR.** We replace Adam/Muon with their Hyperball variants, and use the AUS trajectories recorded from the baseline run as the new LR schedule. As shown in Fig. 2, replaying the AUS trajectories as LR schedules causes the Hyperball optimizers to reproduce nearly identical AUS curves as their base optimizers, indicating that LR in Hyperball implicitly serves as ELR and precisely controls AUS. Moreover, once the AUS trajectories are aligned, the Hyperball optimizers produce similar loss curves to their base optimizers, suggesting that AUS is one of the principal quantities governing training dynamics. ![Clipboard_Screenshot_1785917868.png#center](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/e3076a8f/2026080516182574_c4618616b5a1dd20230e651b39b8205b.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1785917908;2101277908&q-key-time=1785917908;2101277908&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=9da4a8afd6d5134c966ffc4f573182f51d5336a0) *!12 Figure 2. Replaying the AUS trajectories of base optimizers as LR schedules causes Hyperball optimizers to produce nearly identical loss and AUS curves. The top row shows the AUS curves, the middle row shows the loss trajectories, while the bottom row shows their loss differences.!* ::: info **Models Without Scale Invariance.** For a standard GPT-2 model (non-scale invariant), the loss curves still largely overlap, though the loss curve diverged more in the early stages. We attribute this difference to Hyperball fixing the weight norm at a relatively small initialization value, which can be mitigated by carefully tuning the initialization scale. ::: **Enhancing AUS control with tangent momentum.** Let us revisit our second assumption: $\langle \texttt{Opt}_t, \mathbf{w}_t\rangle \approx 0$. Although $\langle \nabla f(\mathbf{w}_t), \mathbf{w}_t\rangle = 0$ holds in scale-invariant models, the momentum $\mathbf{m}_{t}$ may not remain orthogonal to the current weights, as it accumulates gradients from previous iterates. We thus project the momentum onto the tangent space at the current weights: $$\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{m}_{t} = (1 - \beta) \mathbf{m}_{t-1} + \beta \nabla f(\mathbf{w}_t) \\ \texttt{Tangent Momentum: }&\mathbf{m}_{t} ^{\perp} = (I - \widehat{\mathbf{w}}_t\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_t^\top) \mathbf{m}_{t} \\ \end{aligned} $$ We compare vanilla MuonH and MuonH using tangent momentum, namely MuonH-T. In Fig. 3, MuonH-T produces the AUS trajectory that aligns more closely with its LR schedule and achieves a slightly lower validation loss. ![Clipboard_Screenshot_1785920515.png](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/b729e183/2026080517020359_57796dfbc185aeb1018af6ba0c28b9bf.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1785920526;2101280526&q-key-time=1785920526;2101280526&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=32e150f82fc1b01bf00499daa0577157751da75e) *!12 Figure 3. Tangent momentum refines the AUS control of Hyperball optimizers. Both LR schedules and AUS trajectories are shown for MuonH and MuonH-T.!* *In summary*, we define the notion of the AUS and propose to control it via ELR. Interestingly, this perspective leads to the popular Hyperball optimizers. In the remainder of this post, we will use Hyperball optimizers as a testbed to study the properties of ELR.
**Takeaway:** AUS can be explicitly controlled via ELR, and Hyperball optimizers implictly adopts ELR as its normal LR.
# What's Good About ELR? In this section, let us take a closer look at two special properties of ELR. **Property I. ELR enables more accurate predictions of the loss trajectories.** A common experience in pretraining is that if two training runs share similar cumulative LRs $\sum_{i=1}^t\eta_i$, they tend to achieve similar final losses. Motivated by this, *Luo et al. (2025)* [^ref_multi] proposed the *multi-power law (MPL)* model, which predicts the validation loss from the LR schedule. Similar approaches were also noted by *Tissue et al. (2024)* [^ref_anneal] and *Li et al. (2025)* [^ref_fsl]. Let us briefly recap the MPL model. It consists of two terms: one captures the cumulative LR, while the other accounts for the effect of LR decay. The original LR decay term involves complex nonlinear expressions. For simplicity, we adopt a simpler variant that removes this nonlinear component while retaining strong predictive performance. See the equation below: $$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(t) &= L_0 + \underbrace{A \left(\sum_{i=1}^t\eta_i + S_w\right)^{-\alpha}}_{\text{Cum. LR contribution}} - \underbrace{B\sum_{i=1}^t(\eta_{i-1} - \eta_i) }_{\text{LR decay contribution}} \\ &= L_0 + A \left(\sum_{i=1}^t\eta_i + S_w\right)^{-\alpha} - B \eta_t \end{aligned} $$ This model has 4 fitted parameters: $L_0, A, \alpha$, and $B$. Notably, $S_w$ denotes the cumulative LR during warmup, and $i=1$ corresponds to the first step after warmup. To compare the predictive power of LR and ELR, we replace the LR $\eta$ in the MPL model with the ELR $\eta^\star$. We fit both models using 65 Muon runs from a sweep under linear or warm-stable-decay (WSD) schedules. In Fig. 4, we evaluate the MPL models in two settings: - **In-sample fit.** The top row compares the observed validation-loss trajectories with predictions on the runs used for fitting models. The ELR-based models follow the observed trajectories more closely than the LR-based counterparts. - **Held-out generalization.** The bottom row evaluates the MPL models on unseen runs. We hold out each of six runs in turn, re-fit the model on the remaining runs, and predict the losses of the held-out run. The ELR-based predictions align more closely with the observed losses. ![mpl_linear_wsd.png#790px #438px #center](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/b729e183/2026072715031010_6eb18db04f97290dc5483c61bf364d97.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1785135792;2100495792&q-key-time=1785135792;2100495792&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=0d68de462deddd85f493f479f724ec1bbc249568) *!12 Figure 4. Comparison between ELR-based and LR-based MPL models. The top row presents in-sample fit, and the bottom row demonstrates held-out generalization. ELR-based model predicts the loss more accurately across both settings.!* > We note that our experiments consider predictions under the same schedules. In contrast, *Luo et al. (2025)* [^ref_multi] fit their models across multiple schedule shapes and showed generalization to previously unseen ones. Across both settings, ELR consistently yields more accurate loss predictions than LR, suggesting that it better captures the training dynamics. **Property II. ELR transfers more reliably across model scales.** LR transfer is a central challenge in large-scale pretraining. The goal is to tune LRs on smaller models and apply them directly to larger-scale training runs. In *Wen et al. (2026)* [^ref_hyperball], Hyperball optimizers show strong LR transferability across model scales. They attribute this transferability to its direct control over AUS. This raises a natural question: is the hyperspherical constraint necessary, or does ELR alone provide this transferability? To verify this, we consider the update rule in Eq. (2): $$ \mathbf{w}_{t+1} = (1-\eta \lambda )\mathbf{w}_{t} - \eta^\star_t\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t}\Vert \texttt{N}(\texttt{Opt}_t). $$ This rule allows us to tune ELR without constraining the weight norm. We first perform a width-scaling sweep on the scale-invariant GPT-2 model, varying the model width while keeping the other training setup fixed. In Fig. 5, the optimal normal LR shifts noticeably with width, whereas the optimal ELR remains within a much narrower range. We next perform a depth-scaling sweep by varying only the number of layers. Again, the optimal ELR remains stable across depths. Yang et al. (2026) [^ref_jingzhao] also shows that hyperparameter scakubg law for ELR can be more accurate than those for LR. ![width_depth_scaling_val_loss_vs_lr.png#center](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/b729e183/2026072715011567_1a6f01d58f4e63e121f65df5c222903e.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1785135676;2100495676&q-key-time=1785135676;2100495676&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=4956af2bbc17add0c560f2cb07bdcbedc92e5fd7) *!12 Figure 5. Comparison of LR and ELR transferability across model scales. ELR is tuned directly using the update rule in Eq. (2), while LR is tuned using the standard update rule. Muon is used as the base optimizer in both settings.!* We note that the optimal ELR scheme does **not** transfer reliably across different training horizons. More broadly, scheduling ELR exhibits substantially different behavior from scheduling the normal LR. Next, we will delve deeper into ELR scheduling.
**Takeaway:** ELR serves as a more predictive and transferable heuristic than normal LR.

The training run under a linear schedule achieve the lowest training loss.!* **Weight-norm dynamics explain AUS patterns.** Recall $\text{AUS}\approx \frac{\eta_t\Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^{\perp} \Vert }{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1} \Vert}$. When $\Vert \texttt{Opt}_t^{\perp} \Vert$ is approximately constant, the AUS is determined primarily by $\eta_t$ and $\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1} \Vert$. While $\eta_t$ follows LR schedules, recent studies [^ref_spherical] [^ref_intrinsic_lr] suggest that the weight norm usually changes rapidly before settling into a stationary regime. Let us consider gradient descent as a simple example: $\mathbf{w}_{t+1} = (1-\eta \lambda )\mathbf{w}_{t} - \eta \nabla f(\textbf{w}_t).$ For a scale-invariant objective, the weight norm increases whenever $$ \Vert \nabla_{\mathbf{w}_t^{\perp}} f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_t) \Vert\ge\sqrt{\frac{2\lambda}{\eta}}\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t} \Vert^2. $$ At initialization, $\Vert \mathbf{w}_0 \Vert^2$ is typically small relative to the gradient norm, so this condition is readily satisfied and the weight norm grows rapidly, as shown in Fig. 7. At a sufficiently large step $T$, the weight norm becomes stationary and approximately satisfies: $$ \Vert \mathbf{w}_{T} \Vert^2 \approx \sqrt\frac{\eta}{2\lambda } \Vert \nabla_{\mathbf{w}_T^{\perp}} f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_T) \Vert. $$ +++ **Proof Sketch** Recall the scale invariance that $f(c \mathbf{w}) = f(\mathbf{w})$, we have: $$ \nabla f(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{I - \widehat{\mathbf{w}}\widehat{\mathbf{w}}^\top}{\Vert \mathbf{w}\Vert} \nabla f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}) = \frac{1}{\Vert \mathbf{w}\Vert} \nabla_{\mathbf{w}^{\perp}} f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}) $$ The norm of weights updates as follows: $$ \begin{aligned} \Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1} \Vert^2 &= \Vert (1-\eta \lambda )\mathbf{w}_{t} - \eta \nabla f(\textbf{w}_t) \Vert^2 \\ &= (1-\eta \lambda )^2\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t} \Vert^2 + \frac{\eta^2}{\Vert \mathbf{w}_t\Vert^2} \Vert \nabla_{\mathbf{w}_t^{\perp}} f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_t) \Vert^2 \end{aligned} $$ We can then rewrite as: $$ \begin{aligned} \Vert \mathbf{w}_{t+1} \Vert^2 - \Vert \mathbf{w}_{t} \Vert^2 &=(-2\eta\lambda + \eta^2\lambda^2)\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t} \Vert^2 + \frac{\eta^2}{\Vert \mathbf{w}_t\Vert^2} \Vert \nabla_{\mathbf{w}_t^{\perp}} f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_t) \Vert^2 \\ &\ge -2\eta\lambda \Vert \mathbf{w}_{t} \Vert^2 + \frac{\eta^2}{\Vert \mathbf{w}_t\Vert^2} \Vert \nabla_{\mathbf{w}_t^{\perp}} f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_t) \Vert^2 \end{aligned} $$ Hence, a sufficient condition under which the weight norm increases is: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\eta^2}{\Vert \mathbf{w}_t\Vert^2} \Vert \nabla_{\mathbf{w}_t^{\perp}} f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_t) \Vert^2 \ge 2\eta\lambda \Vert \mathbf{w}_{t} \Vert^2 \iff \Vert \nabla_{\mathbf{w}_t^{\perp}} f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_t) \Vert \geq \sqrt{\frac{2\lambda}{\eta}}\Vert \mathbf{w}_{t} \Vert^2 \end{aligned} $$ We can also solve for the stationary weight norm at a sufficiently large training step $T$: $$ \begin{aligned} \Vert \mathbf{w}_{T} \Vert^2 &= (1-\eta \lambda )^2\Vert \mathbf{w}_{T} \Vert^2 + \frac{\eta^2}{\Vert \mathbf{w}_T\Vert^2} \Vert \nabla_{\mathbf{w}_T^{\perp}} f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_T) \Vert^2 \\ &= \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{2\eta \lambda - \eta^2\lambda^2}} \Vert \nabla_{\mathbf{w}_T^{\perp}} f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_T) \Vert \\ & \approx \sqrt\frac{\eta}{2\lambda } \Vert \nabla_{\mathbf{w}_T^{\perp}} f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_T) \Vert \end{aligned} $$ +++ - The stationary weight norm explains the *angular collapse* phenomenon. Substituting $\Vert \mathbf{w}_T \Vert^2$ into the definition of ELR gives $$\text{AUS} \approx \frac{\eta\Vert\nabla_{\mathbf{w}_T^{\perp}} f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_T)\Vert }{\Vert \mathbf{w}_{T} \Vert^2} = \sqrt{2\eta\lambda}. $$ For a fixed $\lambda$, the stationary AUS scales only as $\text{AUS} \propto \sqrt{\eta}$. This square-root scaling makes AUS vary much less than the normal LR, causing the trajectories to collapse. - The evolution of the weight norm also explains the two-phase dynamics. Early in training, the rapid growth of $\Vert \mathbf{w}_t \Vert$ causes AUS to decline earlier than the normal LR, effectively shortening the warmup. Later, as the weight norm stabilizes, AUS becomes increasingly determined by the LR and follows its scheduler shape more closely. **The warmup length and peak value of AUS trajectories scale weakly with the training horizons.** We sweep warmup and peak LR under linear schedules across different training horizons, and present the outperforming runs in Fig. 8. Longer training horizons favor longer warmup phases and substantially lower peak LRs. By contrast, the corresponding AUS trajectories show only a modest increase in warmup length, while the peak value of AUS changes slightly. Hence, we conjecture that the optimal warmup and peak value of ELR schedule can be searched in a much narrower range than those of the normal LR schedule. @@@tabContentCard [[tabs]] label = "Attention A sweep over warmup length and peak LR across different training horizons under linear schedules. The figure shows both LR schedules and the corresponding AUS trajectories for each weight matrix in the last layer. !*
**Takeaway:** AUS exhibits rapid changes early in training and becomes smoother later, following a consistent pattern across model blocks.
# Schedule Your ELR Better! In this section, we design better ELR schedules using Hyperball optimizers. Recall that in Hyperball optimizers, LR implicitly serves as the ELR. **Minus-square-root schedule.** The AUS dynamics motivate an ELR schedule with a shorter warmup, a higher early peak, and a decay that is rapid at first and more gradual later. We therefore consider a power-decay schedule with exponent $p=0.5$, which we call the *minus-square-root schedule*. After a linear warmup of $T_w$ steps, the schedule follows $$ \eta^\star_t = \eta^\star_{\rm peak} \left( 1-\left(\frac{t-T_w}{T-T_w}\right)^p \right) = \eta^\star_{\rm peak} \left( 1-\sqrt{\frac{t-T_w}{T-T_w}} \, \right), \quad T_w\le t\le T. $$ We evaluate this schedule on the modded-nanoGPT Track 3 benchmark. As shown in Fig. 9, MuonH with a well-tuned minus-square-root schedule (MuonH-msqrt)[^ref_muonminus] reaches the target validation loss of 3.28 in 3,175 steps—75 steps earlier than the previous MuonH-linear SOTA. ![Clipboard_Screenshot_1785920475.png](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/b729e183/2026080517011799_122a2fb51e4fd15748986645552f2b55.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1785920480;2101280480&q-key-time=1785920480;2101280480&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=cf002339debccf8b0c732c65c4fb201b9474a9f8) *!12 Figure 9. Results on the modded-nanoGPT Track 3 optimization benchmark. MuonH-msqrt[^ref_muonminus] reaches the target validation loss of 3.28 in 3,175 steps, improving the previous MuonH-linear result by 75 steps. MuonH-power from PR #345[^ref_muonpower][^ref_freelunch] reaches the target in 3,150 steps.!* More importantly, this schedule captures the two patterns identified in the previous section: - **Short warmup and high peak.** The schedule uses a 100-step warmup and a peak value of 0.0300. Compared with the linear baseline, it is a $1.67$x increase. - **Rapid decay and a smoother tail.** After warmup, the ELR initially drops sharply and then becomes gradually closer to a linear schedule towards the end of the training. This shape resembles the AUS trajectories of the best-performing run under the linear schedule in Fig. 7. > PR #345[^ref_muonpower][^ref_freelunch] independently introduces a similar schedule that reaches the target validation loss of 3.28 in 3,150 steps. It uses the same peak value of 0.0300, followed by power decay with exponent $0.4$. This result confirms our earlier insights into ELR scheduling. We next evaluate MuonH-msqrt on a 6B-MoE model trained on ~32.7B tokens and on a scaling ladder covering multiple compute budgets. On the 6B-MoE run in Fig. 10, MuonH-msqrt achieves the lowest validation loss among MuonH-linear, Muon-WSD, and Muon-linear. Across the scaling ladder, it also achieves the lowest final loss at each matched compute budget. However, its fitted scaling slope is slightly shallower, so extrapolating the fitted trends suggests that the advantage of MuonH-msqrt may vanish at larger compute. ![Clipboard_Screenshot_1786085280.png#center](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/e3076a8f/2026080714510838_e0b82c0920759548101b7720085c0c13.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1786085469;2101445469&q-key-time=1786085469;2101445469&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=e3e46047d75656860361f27439c3253aadc42a5c) *!12 Figure 10. Training and validation loss curves for a 6B-MoE model trained on approximately 32.7B tokens (left and middle), together with a scaling ladder over multiple compute budgets (right). MuonH-msqrt achieves the lowest validation loss on the 6B run and the lowest final loss at each measured compute budget.!* **Piecewise-linear schedule.** Although the minus-square-root schedule captures the observed two-phase dynamics, both its early drop and late-stage decay are characterized by a single exponent $\rho$, which is not flexible during tuning. We therefore consider a more flexible *piecewise-linear schedule*. As shown in Fig. 11, this schedule has two phases: - **Early phase: high peak and rapid decay.** Compared with the minus-square-root schedule, the piecewise-linear schedule reaches a higher peak and then drops more sharply to an intermediate point. - **Late phase: exact linear decay.** Starting from the intermediate point, the ELR decays linearly to zero, directly matching the late-stage pattern observed above. Evidently, the piecewise-linear schedule achieves lower training and validation losses than the minus-square-root and linear schedules. ![Clipboard_Screenshot_1785918377.png #center](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/b729e183/2026080516262025_1f6fa6eb5784f4dd44afd7b0ddd29690.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1785918383;2101278383&q-key-time=1785918383;2101278383&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=9ee0835c36811d054f1f32e0c922a7a9f18bece4) *!12 Figure 11. Comparison of linear, minus-square-root, and piecewise-linear schedules with MuonH. The piecewise-linear schedule achieves the best performance.!* :::info **Tuning Intermediate Point in Piecewise-linear Schedule** The piecewise-linear schedule introduces two more hyperparameters: the position and value of the intermediate point. Fig. 12 shows a grid search over the position and value of the intermediate point, where the optimal position appears relatively early in training and at a low value. However, the transferability of this schedule remains an open question. ::: ![Clipboard_Screenshot_1785918334.png #center](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/b729e183/2026080516253621_a578df55dd91f5d5db3daa8a09bf3dac.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1785918339;2101278339&q-key-time=1785918339;2101278339&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=6cfb52104658661f6b4947d95e746c432576894c) *!12 Figure 12. Grid search over the position and value of the intermediate point. Within the evaluated grid, the lowest validation loss is obtained with an intermediate point relatively early in training and at a low value.!* *In summary*, we propose two ELR schedules that amplify the AUS's two-phase pattern. As Hyperball optimizers offer direct control over AUS, they naturally benefit from these schedules and achieve improved performance.
**Takeaway:** Try minus-square-root and piecewise-linear schedules!
# Future Work We believe ELR provides a better heuristic for controlling optimization in LLM pretraining. Compared with LR, ELR captures the AUS, which matters more in LLMs with many scale-invariant weights. Several insights gained from ELR have been applied to the production of our frontier models. Our investigation is only a first step toward this goal. A key open question is why early training tolerates and often benefits from a large peak ELR, whereas later training consistently favors a slower, approximately linear decay. Beyond understanding, we also aim to establish scaling laws for ELR hyperparameters, including the peak value, warmup duration, etc, enabling their reliable transfer across training horizons and model scales. Looking ahead, we envision a transition from normal LR scheduling to ELR scheduling, enabling more direct control over training dynamics, better hyperparameter transfer, and more predictable LLM pretraining. > **Contributors**: Zhanpeng Zhou$^*$, Wenjie Zhou$^*$, Yufei Gu$^*$, Juqiu Wang, Guanwei Zhang$^\dagger$, Ruobing Xie, Xianbiao Qi, Yushi Bai$^\dagger$, Kaifeng Lyu, Shunyu Yao > ($*$: equal contribution;$\dagger$: corresponding author.) # Citation ``` @misc{zhou-zhou-gu-2026-elr, title = {# From LR to ELR: A Better Heuristic for Pretraining Dynamics}, author = {Zhou, Zhanpeng and Zhou, Wenjie and Gu, Yufei and Wang, Juqiu and Zhang, Guanwei and Xie, Ruobing and Qi, Xianbiao and Bai, Yushi and Lyu, Kaifeng and Yao, Shunyu}, year = {2026}, url = {https://hy.tencent.ai/research/elr} } ``` # Acknowledgement We thank the ProdEng team for their technical support. We also thank Jiacheng You, Kairong Luo, Yifeng Liu, Zeke Xie, and Lambert Wong for valuable discussions on optimization theory and the theoretical details of ELR.
